grammar.title: Fronting and Word Order for Emphasis
grammar.explanation:
**Fronting** means moving part of a sentence to the **beginning** to give it emphasis or a dramatic effect. For example, *A castle stood on the hill* becomes ***On the hill stood** a castle*.

Sometimes fronting also changes the word order of the subject and verb. This change is called **inversion**, and it is common in storytelling, speeches, and formal writing.

After a fronted place or direction, a simple verb like **be**, **stand**, **lie**, **come**, or **go** can come **before a noun subject**. For example, ***Into the room walked** a tall man* and ***Next to the door lay** a pile of newspapers*.

With a **pronoun** subject, do not invert. Say *Here **it comes***, never *Here comes it*.

Fronted adjectives and participles follow the pattern adjective plus **be** plus subject, as in ***Gone are** the days* and ***Lucky are** those who have good friends*.

With **so** and **such**, the pattern is **so** plus adjective plus **be** or an auxiliary plus subject plus **that**. For example, ***So loud was** the music **that** we could not hear each other*.

You can also front an object for contrast, and then the rest of the sentence stays in **normal order**. For example, ***Coffee** I love; **tea** I cannot stand*.
examples: ***Here comes** the bus!* (here plus verb plus noun)
***On the top of the hill stood** an old castle.* (place plus verb plus subject)
***Into the room walked** a man in a black coat.* (direction plus verb plus subject)
***Gone are** the days of cheap flights.* (participle fronting)
***So difficult was** the exam **that** only two students passed.* (so plus adjective plus that)
***Such was** his anger **that** he could not speak.* (such plus be plus that)
***Lucky are** those who love their jobs.* (adjective fronting)
***Some things** you just cannot explain.* (object fronting, normal order)
